Are you in the U.S.?

Most major companies have their own trucking schools and will pay you to go to their driving school if you sign on to work for them. I worked for Swift Transportation went to school in Memphis,TN. School was free if I worked for them for 1 year.

I worked for them for a total of 2 years. 10 or 11 months I was Over the road (OTR) meaning I went everywhere. In 10 months I saw 45 states. Then I got on a dedicated run. Dedicated is you are signed on to only run one companies products. So I worked for Swift but then only ran to Sears/Kmart stores. I made more money and had a more regular routine with the dedicated.

Drivers can make $40,000 to $60,000+ per year depending on how much you want to drive. Most of the major companies are going to pay about the same and you have to deal with the same bullshit.

Other options are day cabs meaning you don't sleep in your truck and you are home every day. Like a regular job but driving. They are usually based on hourly pay $18-$25/hr.

There is also hazardous material, tankers, doubles/triples (small trailers linked together), and heavy haul. all of which require special licenses and permits.

If you are looking to ever drive anything professionally go to a truck driving school. You will get great training and a class A,D, and C CDL which means you can drive anything the size of a semi or smaller. If you got just a class B or Class C you can only drive the smaller cube van like truck.

School bus, tanker, and double/triples are just written tests so are easy licensing endorsements to get once you have a CDL.

Haz-mat is also a written test but you also need to be fingerprinted and they do a FBI backround check.

Once on the highway it's surprisingly easy.

For my school it was 21 days in a row of 10-12 hours a day. first 7 days was in class. then 7 days of just backing up. then 7 days on the road. Then out for 6 weeks with a trainer, driving doing normal trucking deliveries. Then you get your own truck. If you fail any one week in school you repeat that week. Trucking school through a company cost about $4,000. Less than a semester in college. So even if you hate it you aren't out a lot of money. And you still have a CDL for a career to fall back on.

Malt liquor, in North America, is beer with high alcohol content. Legally, it often includes any alcoholic beverage with 5% or more alcohol by volume made with malted barley. In common parlance, it is used for high-alcohol beers (6–7% and more) or beer-derived mixes made with ingredients and processes resembling those in American-style lager. This label is subject to the viewpoint of the brewer

Malt liquor is a strong lager or ale in which sugar, corn or other adjuncts are added to the malted barley to boost the total amount of fermentable sugars in the wort, and thus boost the final alcohol concentration without creating a heavier or sweeter taste. These beers tend to be mildly hopped; that is, they are not very bitter. Brewing and legal definitions

Higher alcohol versions, sometimes called "high-gravity" or just "HG", may contain high levels of fusel alcohols, which gives off solvent- or fuel-like aromas and flavors.

Colt 45, St. Ides, Mickey's, Steel Reserve, King Cobra, and Olde English 800 are most closely associated with malt liquors in the United States
